prize_parts.citation: For discoveries on the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its development into incretin-based therapy for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: B025 is the only candidate that all six of us placed first, and the agreement rests on substance. The arc runs from proglucagon processing and the insulinotropic and satiety actions of GLP-1 (Holst, Drucker) to receptor agonists with durable pharmacokinetics (Knudsen) and then to large independent outcome trials showing glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal benefit. Mechanism, proof in patients and population-level consequence are all unusually clear, and the interpretation is stable after decades of replication. I keep Drucker, Holst and Knudsen because together they span physiology, mechanism of action and the step that made the hormone usable in patients. The long-acting analogue work was itself a biochemical insight about half-life and albumin binding, not only an industrial exercise.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real and unresolved. Mojsov's contribution to identifying the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is credited in the candidate, three colleagues include her, and Habener is not on the list at all, so any trio is open to the charge of rewriting history. There is also a framing risk: if the prize is read as basic physiology, Knudsen's seat is hard to defend, and if it is read as drug development, the choice of academic physiologists is hard to defend. A single large field also leaves little room for a second achievement, and unanimous first place should not be mistaken for the absence of an attribution problem.

responses.point: Excludes Knudsen as largely industrial and translational, and takes Mojsov for the active GLP-1(7-36) form.
responses.response: I disagree with leaving Knudsen out. Designing fatty-acid-acylated, albumin-binding analogues that resist DPP-4 and have once-daily to once-weekly kinetics solved the specific biological problem that made native GLP-1 unusable, and that is a discovery in its own right. Without it the prize would honour the physiology but not the reason it changed medicine. I accept that your concern about Mojsov is serious, and I cannot verify the priority claims from the supplied credit. If the committee adopts a pure-physiology framing, Mojsov in place of Knudsen is defensible, but I would want the priority evidence examined before choosing between them.

responses.point: Proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, covering physiology, mechanism and drug, and sees Mojsov and Habener as making allocation contested.
responses.response: I agree with your configuration and with the logic of three seats spanning discovery, mechanism and therapy. I would qualify one point. Calling the long-acting analogues the drug development track understates how much of the added value was mechanistic, so I would not describe the prize as rewarding development alone. Your unresolved question, whether the prize rewards physiology or drug design, is the right one and decides between your trio and El-Manira's. I think the citation should name both parts explicitly so that it is defensible either way.

responses.point: Ranks B009 (cGAS-STING) second as a conceptually broad innate-immunity advance, and accepts that clinical translation is still unproven.
responses.response: I respect the conceptual clarity of cGAS-STING, and I ranked it lower for maturity, not for science. After more than a decade, no approved STING-directed drug exists, and the early agonist and antagonist programmes have been modest. For a prize of this kind I want the consequence for patients or for a general principle of physiology to be established, and here it is still arriving. I also see a five-name credit set, with Ishikawa, Sun and Wu, that we cannot honestly cut to Chen and Barber without losing something. I would revisit it in a few years, and I do not see it displacing B025 or B047 in this discussion.

responses.point: Supports B047 (CAR-T) and B038 with Bamberg, Nagel and Deisseroth, and notes Eshhar's priority is missing from the credited names.
responses.response: On B038 your trio and mine differ in who is dropped, Hegemann or Bamberg, and that difference shows how arbitrary a three-seat limit is for six strong claims. Nagel and Hegemann published the decisive characterisation together, so I would not break that pairing, though Bamberg's early electrophysiology and Boyden's neuronal demonstration are equally exposed by any trio. I share your Eshhar concern on B047, and I place CAR-T above optogenetics only because its medical consequence is direct and the discovery question is cleaner. As a neurologist I should say plainly that my ranking of B038 second does not rest on field familiarity.

responses.point: Ranks HPV VLP vaccines (B014) and TNF blockade (B040) highly, with strong clinical evidence and long maturity.
responses.response: B014 has the clearest evidence of cancer prevention at population level, which counts heavily in its favour. My hesitation is the attribution: Zhou's early death, the parallel Georgetown, Rochester, Queensland and NCI work, and a patent-shaped history all make the trio harder to defend than the data are strong. I also ask whether the committee will see it as overlapping the 2008 HPV prize, though I think the vaccine is a distinct achievement. I would not put it above CAR-T, but I would keep it in view as the best prevention-oriented candidate on the shortlist.

uncertainties: Whether Knudsen or Mojsov should hold the third seat, and whether priority evidence would change that choice
Whether the prize should be framed as physiology, drug design, or both, and how the citation should word that choice
Absence of Habener from the credited names limits the configurations available
Whether a methods prize (B038) belongs in the discovery remit, and whether any trio from six names is defensible
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I worked with Paul Greengard and have about twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann (a committee colleague, on dopamine neurons, Nurr1 and autophagy), but none of the shortlisted candidates involves them or me. My neurology background overlaps with B038, and I do not treat that as a preference.
